learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Upgrades, Migration, and Version Compatibility.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Upgrades, Migration, and Version Compatibility. Its primary job is to help you set recovery objectives, choose an appropriate backup type, restore into isolation and verify recoverability. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing upgrades, migration, and version compatibility teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: set recovery objectives, choose an appropriate backup type, restore into isolation and verify recoverability. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

items.title: Minor versus major version upgrades pg_upgrade concepts
items.text: Relate this point to upgrades, migration, and version compatibility: define the expected behavior, one edge case, and a query or check that would provide evidence.

items.title: Logical migration strategies
items.text: Prefer additive changes first, test against populated sample data, and preserve compatibility while old and new code overlap.

items.title: Extension compatibility
items.text: Prefer additive changes first, test against populated sample data, and preserve compatibility while old and new code overlap.

items.title: Upgrade testing, rollback planning, and post-upgrade verification
items.text: Mark the transaction boundary explicitly and verify both the commit path and a rollback path in a disposable database.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Upgrades, Migration, and Version Compatibility
content_blocks.code: ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN marketing_opt_in boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false;
content_blocks.expected_output: Existing rows receive the default according to PostgreSQL semantics; verify lock and rewrite characteristics for the actual version and table.
content_blocks.safety_note: Schema changes can lock or rewrite data; rehearsal and rollback planning are required.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run only in a local migration test against representative populated data.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Version note: PostgreSQL 18.6 is the primary reference. PostgreSQL 19 beta/development features are not assumed to be stable.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Upgrades, Migration, and Version Compatibility”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Minor versus major version upgrades pg_upgrade concepts”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Minor versus major version upgrades pg_upgrade concepts”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Upgrades, Migration, and Version Compatibility, with an explanation of “Minor versus major version upgrades pg_upgrade concepts”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Upgrades, Migration, and Version Compatibility fits into the broader goal to set recovery objectives, choose an appropriate backup type, restore into isolation and verify recoverability.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Minor versus major version upgrades pg_upgrade concepts, Logical migration strategies, Extension compatibility.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
